context: Split the two questions the canary conflates. Direction-aware staleness detection answers 'is the mirror behind', and a separate scan of published-results answers 'is the public branch leaking', which is the harm. The second does not depend on develop at all.
description: corpus-drift-check.yml compares with git diff --name-only FETCH_HEAD HEAD, which reports differences in either direction, then unconditionally reports that published-results is behind develop and recommends running the sync workflow. Community submissions land on published-results, so the first one makes the canary fire and advise an action that removes it. It also excludes nothing for legacy submission-manifest.json files. Deeper: the canary tests staleness, but the incident it was built for was a leak. A scheduled job running find_public_path_leaks against published-results itself would have caught all 183 leaking bundles directly, without depending on the two branches being comparable.

preserves.behavior: A recommendation the canary prints must never be an action that deletes public content
Stays report-only; it must not gain write access to a public branch
Stays scheduled rather than push-triggered - dropped push events are the root cause it exists for
Still fires when develop is genuinely ahead - that is the leak this canary exists to catch
